lead: A three-phase AC voltage controller sets the RMS voltage reaching a three-phase load by delaying thyristor firing in every cycle. It exists because three-phase heaters, soft starters and capacitor-bank switches need smooth, lossless voltage control without a transformer tap changer. The three phases interact: in a three-wire star or delta load there is no neutral wire, so the three load currents must add to zero. In a three-wire star, changing the firing angle of one phase changes the voltages of the other two. This chapter covers the three common connections and their firing range.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.1 for the single-phase controller, Unit 1 for SCR pairs, and Unit 2 for three-phase source quantities.

blocks.text: A three-phase AC voltage controller is three thyristor pairs, one in each phase or branch. The pairs can be anti-parallel SCRs or, at low power, TRIACs (see Chapter 5.2). The connection decides whether the phases are independent.

Four-wire star: three separate single-phase controllers with the neutral brought out. Each phase sees its own pair and its own return through the neutral. Set α from 0° to 180° in each phase independently. The neutral carries the sum of the three phase currents, including zero-sequence current. Use this for unbalanced loads or when each phase must be trimmed.

Three-wire star: six thyristors feed a star load with no neutral wire. The three load currents must add to zero at every instant. A change in one firing angle shifts the star point and changes the voltages on the other two phases. For a balanced load, fire all six devices symmetrically with the same α.

Delta: six thyristors sit in the three branches of a delta load. Each branch voltage is a line-to-line voltage. The line current is the difference of two branch currents. This connection is used for high-current loads. Triplen currents can circulate inside the delta instead of entering the supply lines. Some syllabi call the whole family a three-phase AC voltage regulator.

sections.h3: Firing range for a resistive star load

blocks.text: Take a balanced star load of resistance R per phase and a supply with RMS line voltage V_L. For 0 ≤ α ≤ 60°, the RMS load phase voltage is:

blocks.where: V_o,ph is the RMS phase voltage across the load; V_ph is the RMS supply phase voltage V_L/√3; α is the firing angle in radians; this form holds for 0 ≤ α ≤ 60°.

blocks.text: At α = 0 the load phase voltage is the full supply phase voltage. As α rises to 60°, conduction stays continuous, with at least two devices conducting, but the RMS voltage falls. At α = 60° it is about 84% of full. Above 60°, gaps appear, the current becomes discontinuous, and the RMS falls faster. At α = 150° the output reaches zero. The usable range is therefore 0° to 150°, not 0° to 180°.

In the four-wire star each phase is independent and α can go to 180°. In the delta, each branch pair sees the line-to-line voltage and behaves as a single-phase controller: conduction stays continuous up to α = 90°, and the branch output falls to zero at α = 180°. The 60° and 150° landmarks belong to the three-wire star, not to the delta. Do not apply the single-phase RMS formula to one phase of a three-wire star. The floating star point makes the three phase voltages a set, not three separate outputs. An inductive load shifts the extinction angles; the resistive case is the exam standard.

Symmetrical firing uses the same α for all six devices. The three phase currents stay balanced. With symmetrical firing in a balanced three-phase load, the line currents contain harmonics of order 6k ± 1: 5th, 7th, 11th, 13th and so on. Triplen orders (3rd, 9th, 15th) are the zero-sequence family, discussed next. In a three-wire star or delta load, triplen harmonics (3rd, 9th, 15th) are absent from the line currents. A triplen harmonic is in phase in all three phases. Its sum is not zero, so it needs a neutral return. With no neutral, it cannot flow in the lines. In a four-wire star it returns in the neutral; in a delta it circulates in the delta.

Asymmetrical firing uses different α values in different phases or half-cycles. It can produce a DC component and triplen currents. Use it only where a neutral or delta path can absorb the zero-sequence current, or for a short start where the DC component is acceptable.

Uses: three-phase resistance heaters, motor soft starters, and static switches for capacitor banks. A soft starter starts with a large firing angle (near 180°) and reduces it slowly toward 0°, so the motor voltage ramps up from a small value without a large inrush current. A static switch turns a capacitor bank on and off without contact wear. Link to Chapter 5.4 for PWM control.

examples.question: A 415 V, 50 Hz, three-phase supply feeds a star-connected resistive load of 10 Ω per phase through a three-phase AC voltage controller. (a) For α = 60°, find the RMS phase voltage, the line current and the total power. (b) At what firing angle does the output fall to zero?
steps: The supply phase voltage is V_ph = 415/√3 = 239.60 V.
At α = 60° = π/3 rad, conduction is just continuous. Use the resistive star formula: V_o,ph = V_ph × √[1 − (3α/2π) + (3 sin 2α)/(4π)].
In star, line current equals phase current: I = V_o,ph/R = 201.43/10 = 20.14 A.
Power per phase = V_o,ph²/R = 201.43²/10 = 4057.4 W. Total power = 3 × 4057.4 = 12172 W = 12.17 kW.
The output reaches zero at α = 150°.
examples.answer: V_o,ph = 201.43 V, I = 20.14 A, P = 12.17 kW; the output falls to zero at α = 150°.
examples.check:
import math
V_L = 415.0
R = 10.0
alpha = math.pi / 3
V_ph = V_L / math.sqrt(3)
V_o = V_ph * math.sqrt(1 - (3*alpha)/(2*math.pi) + (3*math.sin(2*alpha))/(4*math.pi))
I = V_o / R
P_kW = 3 * V_o**2 / R / 1000
print(round(V_o, 2))
print(round(I, 2))
print(round(P_kW, 2))
print(150.0)

traps: Using the single-phase controller formula on each phase of a three-wire star. With no neutral the phase currents must sum to zero; the star point moves.
Calling α = 60° the full-voltage point. It is only the edge of continuous conduction; the RMS phase voltage is about 84% of the supply phase voltage.

Thinking the output falls to zero at α = 180° in a three-wire star. The zero point is α = 150° because a firing pulse at that instant comes after the relevant line-to-line voltage has already reversed, so no pair of devices can be turned on and no current can start.
Mixing line and phase quantities. In star, line current equals phase current, but line voltage is √3 times phase voltage. In delta, line current is not the branch current.
Expecting triplen harmonics in the line currents of a three-wire load. They need a neutral or a delta path.

quiz.q: State the firing-angle range over which a three-wire star resistive load has continuous conduction and the angle at which the output becomes zero.
quiz.a: Continuous conduction from 0° to 60°; output becomes zero at 150°.

quiz.q: Why can the three phases of a three-wire star controller not be controlled independently?
quiz.a: There is no neutral wire, so the three load currents must sum to zero. Changing one firing angle moves the star point and changes the other phase voltages.

quiz.q: A 400 V, 50 Hz three-phase supply feeds a star-connected 20 Ω per phase resistive load through a three-phase controller. At α = 0°, find the RMS phase voltage, line current and total power.
Why do 3rd and 9th harmonics not appear in the line currents of a three-wire star load?
quiz.a: Triplen harmonics are in phase in all three phases. Their sum is nonzero and needs a neutral return. With no neutral they cannot flow in the line currents.

quiz.q: At α = 120° in a three-wire star resistive load, is the output zero? Explain in one sentence.
quiz.a: No. Conduction is discontinuous but not zero; zero occurs at α = 150°.

quiz.q: A three-wire star controller has one phase pair fired at α = 60° and another at α = 120°. Describe the effect on the load voltages and currents.
quiz.a: The load is unbalanced. The floating star point shifts, so the three phase voltages are no longer the supply phase voltages and contain a zero-sequence (triplen) component. The line currents still sum to zero, so they can carry no zero-sequence current; only their DC and 5th, 7th, 11th … components change.

quiz.q: A delta-connected resistive load has 30 Ω per branch and a 415 V line-line supply. At α = 0°, find the branch current and total power.
quiz.a: At α = 0° the branch gets full line voltage. I_branch = 415/30 = 13.83 A. P = 3 × 415²/30 = 17.22 kW.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial soft starters combine three-phase SCR modules with bypass contactors and closed-loop current control, so the motor sees a controlled voltage ramp. Research versions use digital firing, integrated gate drive and power-factor correction. Search for 'three-phase AC voltage controller RMS formula', 'SCR soft starter' and 'triplen harmonic neutral current'.
